content: Critical care nursing is a specialized field of nursing that focuses on providing care to critically ill or unstable patients. Critical care nurses work in various settings, including emergency departments and intensive care units, where they manage patients with complex and life-threatening conditions. In the United States, most critical care nurses are registered nurses (RNs). Licensed Practical Nurses (LPNs) or Licensed Vocational Nurses (LVNs) are rarely employed in primary care roles within intensive care units due to the complexity and instability of the patient population. However, with appropriate training and experience, LPNs/LVNs can contribute significantly to bedside care for critically ill patients. Nurses in the U.S. who wish to specialize in critical care can pursue certification through the American Association of Critical-Care Nurses (AACN). This organization establishes and maintains standards for critical care nursing. The certification, known as CCRN, is available for nurses caring for adult, pediatric, and neonatal populations. Contrary to popular belief, CCRN does not stand for Critical Care Registered Nurse but rather signifies certification in critical care nursing. It is important to note that all nurses in the U.S. are registered as general nurses without a specialty, and the CCRN is a post-registration specialty certification. The AACN also offers additional certifications for nurses in related areas, such as Progressive Care (PCCN), Cardiac Medicine (CMC), and Cardiac Surgery (CSC). Clinical Nurse Specialists (CNS) can obtain certifications in adult, neonatal, and pediatric acute and critical care (CCNS). In 2007, the AACN introduced the ACNPC certification, an advanced practice credential for Acute Care Nurse Practitioners. These certifications do not grant additional practice privileges, as nursing practice is regulated by state boards of nursing. However, they are highly valued by employers and peers as they demonstrate advanced knowledge, expertise, and a commitment to professional development in critical care nursing. Critical care nurses must be proficient in using a wide range of advanced medical technologies. These include hemodynamic and cardiac monitoring systems, mechanical ventilators, intra-aortic balloon pumps (IABP), ventricular assist devices (LVAD and RVAD), continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT/CVVHDF), extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), and other life-support devices. Training for these technologies is provided through hospital in-services, manufacturer-led sessions, and hands-on education with experienced operators. Many intensive care units also support their staff by sending them to conferences to stay informed about advancements in this rapidly evolving field. Critical care nurses work in diverse environments and care for a wide range of patient populations. They are commonly employed in hospital intensive care units, post-operative care units, and high-dependency units. They may also serve on medical evacuation and transport teams. For example, in 2004, Massachusetts General Hospital collaborated with The Boston Globe to provide an in-depth look at critical care nursing. Reporters spent eight months shadowing nurses in the Surgical Intensive Care Unit (SICU), resulting in a detailed four-part series published in 2005. Critical care nursing encompasses several subspecialties, including Neonatal Intensive Care (NICU), Pediatric Intensive Care (PICU), and Adult Intensive Care (ICU). These subspecialties are generally defined by the age of the patient population. The NICU primarily cares for newborns and premature infants, typically up to one month of age. After this period, care transitions to the PICU, which manages patients from one month to eighteen years old. Patients older than eighteen are usually admitted to the Adult ICU. However, exceptions are made based on individual cases. For instance, a newborn admitted from the Emergency Department may be placed in the PICU rather than the NICU. Similarly, a large adolescent patient may be admitted to the Adult ICU, and adult patients with congenital heart defects may be treated in the PICU if their care team has specialized expertise in their condition. Further specialization within critical care nursing is often based on the specific condition or injury of the patient population. For example, an Adult Trauma Intensive Care Unit focuses on managing adult patients with traumatic injuries. The treatment approaches and care strategies differ significantly between adult and pediatric/neonatal populations, necessitating specialized training and expertise for each subspecialty.
